1.title: Debugging, Evals and Error Handling
1.text: Welcome to Module sixteen: Debugging, Evals and Error Handling. This module covers the skills debugging and error handling. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. Identifying error types and choosing a recovery strategy. Trace analysis to find failure modes. Isolating the origin of a problem: integration layer or model output. Evals: success criteria, design principles and grading.

1.title: Case Check-In: Tidewater's Assistant "Stopped Working"
1.text: Our running case is Tidewater Insurance. Tidewater's Assistant "Stopped Working". Complaint one: "No answers at all since this morning". Complaint two: "Answers are wrong about deductibles for some policies". Complaint three: "Some replies are cut off".

1.title: Step 1: classify the failure
1.text: Step one: classify the failure. The figure shows this: Triage: first the H T T P result, then completeness and parsing, then content quality.

1.title: Step 1: classify the failure, continued
1.text: Step one: classify the failure, continued. four X X (four hundred, four hundred one, four hundred three, four hundred four, four hundred thirteen). Likely origin: Integration: bad request, key, permission, size. Recovery: Fix the request or configuration; retrying unchanged will not help. four hundred twenty-nine. Likely origin: Rate limit. Recovery: Back off, honor retry-after, lower concurrency, spread load. five X X, timeout, overloaded. Likely origin: Transient platform condition. Recovery: Retry with exponential backoff and jitter; fall back or queue. stop reason: max tokens or cut-off text. Likely origin: Output limit. Recovery: Raise max tokens, ask for shorter output, or continue. Jason (Java Script Object Notation) fails to parse or schema violation. Likely origin: Output format. Recovery: Structured output, defensive parsing, retry with the error. Tool errors. Likely origin: Tool or its inputs. Recovery: Fix the tool; return clear is error results.

1.title: Step 1: classify the failure, continued
1.text: Step one: classify the failure, continued. Plausible but wrong content. Likely origin: Model output: prompt, context or data. Recovery: Check the input the model actually saw; grounding, examples, evals. Slow or costly. Likely origin: Context bloat, model or effort too high. Recovery: Prune context, cache, route, lower effort.

1.title: Step 2: use traces
1.text: Step two: use traces. Log for every call: request I D, model, parameters, the full prompt actually sent (with sensitive data masked), tool calls and results, usage, stop reason, latency and the final output. Trace analysis reads these records end to end to see where the chain went wrong: wrong context retrieved, a tool returned bad data, the prompt dropped a rule, or the parser rejected a valid reply.

1.title: Step 3: isolate the origin
1.text: Step three: isolate the origin. The figure shows this: Separate the integration layer from the model output: replay the exact request, check what the model received, and test each layer on its own. Replay the exact request (same prompt, context and parameters). If the bad output reproduces, the cause is the prompt, context or model behavior; if the request itself was malformed or lost data on the way (a truncated history, a missing document, wrong serialization), the cause is the integration layer.

1.title: Step 3: isolate the origin, continued
1.text: Step three: isolate the origin, continued. Check what the model actually received: most "model mistakes" turn out to be missing, stale or truncated input. Change one variable at a time and compare. Exam tip: "Wrong answers" are often wrong or missing input. Look at the logged prompt and tool results before rewriting the prompt or switching models. Exam tip: Check what the model actually received (the logged prompt and tool results) before changing the prompt or the model.

1.title: Evals
1.text: Evals. An eval is a repeatable test that measures quality on representative inputs. Without evals you cannot tell whether a prompt, model or setting change helped or hurt.

1.title: Evals, continued
1.text: Evals, continued. Success criteria. Define them first and make them measurable: task fidelity, consistency, latency, cost, safety. Design principles. Task-specific (mirror real inputs, include edge cases), automate where possible, volume over perfect quality (many automatically graded cases beat few hand-graded ones). Grading. Code-based (exact or string match: fastest, most reliable); human (best nuance, slow and costly); L L M (large language model)-based (fast and scalable for complex judgments: needs a clear rubric, a specific output such as correct or incorrect, optional reasoning, and a reliability check first).

1.title: Evals, continued
1.text: Evals, continued. Use. Run on every change (prompt, model, tool, config), in C I; track regressions; keep a set of past failures as regression tests.

1.title: Evals, continued
1.text: Evals, continued. The figure shows this: The eval loop: define success, build cases, grade, compare versions, fix and re-run. Exam tip: Choose the grading method by need: exact answers to code-based; open-ended quality to L L M-based with a rubric (validated against human judgment); final high-stakes calibration to human review.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. four X X: Fix the request; do not retry unchanged. four hundred twenty-nine: Back off, retry-after, lower concurrency. five X X or overloaded or timeout: Retry with exponential backoff and jitter. max tokens: Cut-off output: raise limit or continue. Parsing: Structured output, defensive parsing, retry with error. Wrong content: Check what the model saw (prompt, context, tool data) first. Traces: Request I D, prompt, tools, usage, stop reason, latency (mask sensitive data). Isolate: Replay the exact request; integration layer versus model output. Evals: Criteria first; task-specific with edge cases; automate; code, human or L L M grading; run on every change.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Requests suddenly return H T T P four hundred one. What should the team do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. four X X authentication errors need a configuration fix, not retries.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. During peak hours some calls return four hundred twenty-nine with retry-after. What is the best response? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Rate limits call for waiting and lower request rates.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. An intermittent five hundred twenty-nine overloaded response appears. What recovery fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Overload is transient; backoff and fallback handle it.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Answers about deductibles are wrong for some policies. The logged prompt shows the policy text was truncated before it reached Claude. Where is the origin? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. The model never saw the needed text; fixing the data path fixes the answer.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Select two. Which two belong in a useful trace of each model call? The five options are on the screen. The answers are C and D. End-to-end traces with identifiers, inputs, usage and stop reasons allow failure analysis (with sensitive data masked).

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all five answers. Question one: A. Question two: A. Question three: C. Question four: B. Question five: C and D. In the next module, we continue the course.
